review_status: draft; dental and orthodontic clinician review required

sources.title: Management of the developing dentition and occlusion, revision 2024
Risks of orthodontic treatment: guidance on informing patients, 2024

options.name: Fixed braces
options.overview: Brackets and an archwire move teeth under an orthodontist's planned, monitored care. They may be one part of a broader bite-management plan.
benefits: Can improve the alignment of selected crowded or rotated teeth
Can address several dental alignment goals within one supervised plan
Remain attached, so daily tray insertion is not required
tradeoffs: Cleaning around brackets and wires takes extra attention
Soreness, rubbing, and appliance breakages can occur
Some jaw discrepancies need additional approaches beyond tooth alignment
clinician_checks: Confirm dental diagnosis, bite relationships, and treatment goals
Assess tooth, root, bone, and gum health using appropriate records
Discuss individual risks, visits, and retention before treatment

options.name: Clear aligners
options.overview: A clinician-planned sequence of removable trays can move selected teeth. Suitability depends on the actual bite, required movements, and oral health.
benefits: Usually less conspicuous than visible fixed brackets
Can be removed for meals and tooth cleaning
Can address selected spacing, crowding, and bite concerns
tradeoffs: Results depend on following the prescribed wear routine
Attachments, additional stages, or fixed braces may still be needed
Removable appliances still carry tooth-movement, decay, and gum-care risks
clinician_checks: Assess whether the required movements are suitable for trays
Check teeth and gums before making treatment scans
Review the person's ability to manage wear, cleaning, and follow-up

options.name: Space assessment and management
options.overview: A dental team may preserve, recover, or redistribute space according to dentition and tooth development. This is a planning category, not a recommendation to remove teeth.
benefits: May preserve room after selected premature primary-tooth losses
May support a developing permanent tooth's eruption path
Can coordinate space with later alignment or tooth replacement
tradeoffs: Space-maintaining appliances can collect plaque, loosen, or break
Some proposed methods are irreversible and need separate risk discussion
Evidence and outcomes vary; later orthodontic treatment may still be needed
clinician_checks: Complete a space analysis and short- and long-term plan
Confirm tooth number, eruption status, and successor development
Review hygiene, bite, growth, and capacity for follow-up

options.name: Functional appliances during growth
options.overview: For selected growing patients with a Class II problem, a clinician may use a functional appliance to change the bite, mainly through dental changes. It does not guarantee permanent jaw-growth alteration.
benefits: May reduce excessive upper-incisor projection in suitable cases
May improve the relationship between upper and lower front teeth
Dental repositioning may improve upper-lip coverage of the front teeth
tradeoffs: Response varies and depends on cooperation with appliance wear
A later or combined fixed-brace phase may be needed
Long-term changes in jaw size or position cannot be promised
clinician_checks: Assess remaining growth and the actual Class II pattern
Review incisor inclination, oral health, and functional concerns
Discuss realistic goals and alternative pathways

options.name: Specialist jaw-surgery assessment
options.overview: An orthodontist and maxillofacial surgeon may assess selected skeletal discrepancies that tooth movement alone cannot address. A case label or photograph does not establish a need for surgery.
benefits: Can address jaw relationships beyond tooth alignment alone
May improve biting and chewing in selected patients
May improve facial balance when this is an agreed treatment goal
tradeoffs: Involves an operation, general anaesthetic, and recovery
Sensory changes can persist; individual surgical risks require discussion
Coordinated orthodontic and surgical care can be lengthy and demanding
clinician_checks: Confirm the skeletal problem using examination and justified records
Assess growth, health, expectations, and alternatives together
Explain individualized risks, likely changes, and consent

options.name: Combined dental and specialist care
options.overview: Some confirmed findings need coordinated orthodontic, restorative, periodontal, or oral-surgery input. The sequence depends on the cause, disease status, and the person's goals.
benefits: Coordinates gum and tooth health with alignment decisions
Can plan spacing alongside the shape or replacement of teeth
Allows specialist discussion of impacted teeth and other complex findings
tradeoffs: Several clinicians or stages may be involved
A chosen pathway may include irreversible procedures and additional risks
Not every gap, tooth difference, or visible gum display needs correction
clinician_checks: Identify the confirmed cause and stabilize active disease
Agree responsibilities and sequence across the treating team
Discuss intervention, monitoring, and no-treatment alternatives

options.name: Retention and maintenance
options.overview: Fixed or removable retainers help maintain positions after active treatment. A retainer is not automatically a treatment for new crowding or a substitute for review.
benefits: Helps limit unwanted positional changes after treatment
Supports maintenance of agreed alignment goals
Fixed and removable designs offer different care arrangements
tradeoffs: Removable designs depend on consistent prescribed wear
Fixed designs need careful cleaning and checks for bond failure
Repair, replacement, and ongoing review may be needed
clinician_checks: Check current alignment, gum health, and retainer fit
Review integrity and cleaning access for fixed retainers
Discuss the individualized maintenance plan and signs of change

options.name: Clinician-led observation
options.overview: After examination, a clinician may advise no active treatment now, with planned review of development or changes. Observation is a deliberate option, not an automatic conclusion from a photo.
benefits: Can avoid unnecessary intervention when treatment is not indicated
Allows tooth eruption and development to be reviewed over time
Preserves the option to reconsider care as findings change
tradeoffs: Does not actively straighten teeth or alter the bite
New symptoms or changes may require earlier reassessment
Missing review visits can delay recognition of a changing problem
clinician_checks: Confirm that observation is appropriate for the actual finding
Set individualized review arrangements and escalation signs
Record the person's concerns and reasons for the chosen approach

shared_risks: Root resorption: roots can shorten during orthodontic movement; significant changes can affect tooth support and require clinical monitoring.
Decalcification and caries: plaque around fixed or removable appliances can contribute to white spots and tooth decay; prevention and review matter.
Gum and periodontal health: inflammation, recession, or support loss can occur; active disease needs clinician-led stabilization before tooth movement.
Relapse: teeth can change position after treatment; discuss retention and ongoing review as part of the plan.
pathway_note: These are general discussion pathways with potential benefits and tradeoffs, not personalized treatment recommendations. Case links are educational associations; they do not determine candidacy. Only a qualified treating clinician can select an appropriate approach after examination and suitable records. A photograph cannot establish root and bone status, remaining growth, or treatment suitability. A rendered correction is an illustration, not a prediction, guarantee, appliance prescription, or movement schedule.
